🚨 [AI SECURITY / MODEL DISTILLATION] — U.S. OFFICIALS ACCUSE SIX CHINESE AI COMPANIES OF TARGETING AMERICAN FRONTIER MODELS WITH "INDUSTRIAL-SCALE" DISTILLATION  DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba are among companies named in the allegation.  The American models allegedly targeted include technology from:  ANTHROPIC OPENAI GOOGLE SPACEX.  CyberSignal AI Priority: 🔴 VERY HIGH  🇺🇸 Source: U.S. law-enforcement + intelligence officials 🇨🇳 Companies named include: DeepSeek · Moonshot AI · Alibaba 🧠 Technique: Model distillation 🎯 Alleged targets: Anthropic · OpenAI · Google · SpaceX models ⚔️ U.S. claim: Aggressive, targeted activity at industrial scale 📅 DISCLOSED: September 8, 2026  The frontier-AI race now has another security boundary:  THE OUTPUT OF THE MODEL ITSELF.  ### 🔎 What happened  U.S. officials accused six China-based AI companies of systematically querying American AI systems and using the resulting outputs to accelerate development of competing models.  The technique is known as:  DISTILLATION.  At a basic level:  LARGE / EXPENSIVE MODEL ↓ generates high-quality outputs ↓ outputs become training signal ↓ smaller / cheaper model learns patterns ↓ new model reproduces part of teacher capability.  Distillation itself is:  A LEGITIMATE MACHINE-LEARNING TECHNIQUE.  The dispute is over:  HOW THE TRAINING DATA WAS OBTAINED  and:  WHETHER PROVIDER RULES / INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY WERE VIOLATED.  ### ⚔️ Alleged operation  Access American frontier AI service ↓ Generate large volumes of model outputs ↓ Collect reasoning / response patterns ↓ Construct synthetic training corpus ↓ Train domestic models ↓ Reproduce capabilities at lower training cost ↓ Accelerate competing AI development  U.S. officials characterized the alleged activity as:  "AGGRESSIVE, MALICIOUS AND TARGETED DISTILLATION ACTIVITIES AT AN INDUSTRIAL SCALE."  ### 🎯 Companies named  Reuters reports that the U.S. statement names:  SIX CHINESE AI COMPANIES.  Those identified publicly in reporting include:  DEEPSEEK  MOONSHOT AI  ALIBABA.  The alleged American targets include model variants from:  ANTHROPIC  OPENAI  GOOGLE  SPACEX.  ### 🧠 Why distillation matters  Frontier models can cost:  ENORMOUS SUMS  to train from scratch.  If another company can extract useful behavior by generating millions of carefully designed outputs from an existing model, it may reduce:  R&D TIME EXPERIMENTATION COST TRAINING COST DATA-CREATION COST.  This turns the model API itself into something resembling:  A HIGH-VALUE INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY INTERFACE.  ### 🔐 The AI security problem  Traditional API security asks:  IS THIS USER AUTHORIZED?  AI security increasingly also has to ask:  WHAT IS AN AUTHORIZED USER LEARNING FROM THE MODEL AT SCALE?  Because an account can make technically valid requests while collectively performing:  CAPABILITY EXTRACTION.  That creates detection problems resembling:  DATA EXFILTRATION  but in reverse.  Instead of stealing files from the server:  THE ATTACKER MAY BE EXTRACTING BEHAVIOR THROUGH OUTPUTS.  ### 🛡️ What AI providers can monitor  Signals potentially associated with extraction campaigns include:  → unusually high query volume → systematic prompt families → requests designed to map specific capability boundaries → large distributed account pools → repetitive benchmark-style questioning → coordinated IP / identity infrastructure → generation patterns inconsistent with normal product usage → rapid harvesting across model versions  Providers can respond with:  rate limits behavioral detection account clustering output controls watermarking / provenance research terms enforcement.  ### ⚔️ National-security dimension  The U.S. statement goes significantly further than:  COMMERCIAL IP THEFT.  Officials claim that reducing the cost of Chinese AI development could also improve China's:  MILITARY  and:  CYBERATTACK  capabilities.  That is why model distillation is increasingly entering the same policy debate as:  ADVANCED CHIP EXPORT CONTROLS.  The strategic resources are becoming:  COMPUTE + MODEL WEIGHTS + MODEL OUTPUTS.  ### ⚠️ Important caveat  THIS IS AN ACCUSATION FROM THE U.S. GOVERNMENT.  It should NOT be written as:  “DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba were proven to have stolen American AI.”  Reuters reported that the Chinese embassy in Washington had not immediately responded to the new allegations.  Distillation itself is also common and legitimate in machine learning.  The disputed conduct concerns alleged:  TARGETED EXTRACTION  of capabilities from American systems at industrial scale.  The U.S. statement says the activity occurred:  “likely with Chinese government awareness.”  That is also an:  ASSESSMENT.  Not publicly presented proof of direct government ordering.  ### 🧠 Why this matters  Cybersecurity spent decades learning how to protect:  SOURCE CODE DATABASES CREDENTIALS TRADE SECRETS.  Frontier AI adds another asset:  MODEL BEHAVIOR.  You do not necessarily need to steal:  THE WEIGHTS  if enough carefully chosen queries can transfer part of:  WHAT THE MODEL KNOWS HOW TO DO.  ### 🧠 CyberSignal Insight  THE AI SECURITY PERIMETER DOES NOT END AT THE MODEL WEIGHTS.  EVERY OUTPUT IS A SMALL PIECE OF CAPABILITY LEAVING THE SYSTEM.  ONE RESPONSE IS A PRODUCT.  MILLIONS OF SYSTEMATIC RESPONSES CAN BECOME:  TRAINING DATA.  Sources: U.S. law-enforcement and intelligence officials · Reuters

⚡️ 0-Day Alert: Chrome v8 RCE exploited in the wild  CVE-2026-85046: v8 array-builtin callback side-effect to elements-kind transition confusion. Affects both Turbofan and Maglev.  Exploit will work in default config but requires multiple other bugs to achieve arbitrary code execution on the system. The bug alone without helpers could do for an UXSS.  Patched in Chrome 152.0.7977.82/.83

A browser update can be deployed successfully and still leave the vulnerable code running.  That distinction matters with CVE-2026-85046. Google fixed the actively exploited V8 type-confusion flaw in Chrome 152.0.7977.82 for Linux, but a package update is only one step in remediation. If users leave existing Chrome or Chromium processes open, the old executable image can remain resident in memory.  This is the kind of gap that turns a clean patch-management dashboard into false confidence. A fleet can be “compliant” on paper while part of the user population is still executing the vulnerable browser.  **In practical terms, it is a good time to:** - compare deployed package versions with the browser versions actually running on representative endpoints - identify Chrome or Chromium processes whose start times predate the package update - require or validate browser restarts after the security update - sample offline and intermittently connected Linux laptops that may have missed deployment - verify the live version from Chrome or Chromium after restart rather than trusting deployment status alone  How many patching programs verify the running process, rather than stopping at the installed package?  #LinuxSecurity #VulnerabilityManagement #SysAdmin #IncidentResponse linuxsecurity.com/news/secur…

sample_tweets.text: Microsoft developed the Cloud web applications threat matrix to organize relevant techniques across cloud-hosted web applications and serverless platforms using MITRE ATT&CK tactics. msft.it/6015ak507  The matrix can help security teams assess visibility gaps, prioritize hardening, and plan investigations across application code, managed runtimes, workload identities, deployment pipelines, and connected cloud resources.  Read the blog to learn more about the framework, the technique catalog, and guidance for reducing exposure across cloud-native environments.

[論文]サイバーセキュリティの質問に、検索して得た情報を根拠として答えるRAG（検索拡張生成）方式「MITRE-SAGE」の提案。イランのギーラン大学のプレプリントで、MITRE-ATT&CKなどから構築した知識グラフ、関連文書、Web検索の3系統を7体のAIエージェントで使い分ける構成。統括役にQwen2[.]5-14B、下位のエージェントにQwen2[.]5-7Bを置き、いずれも8ビット量子化した軽量構成。著者らが新設した3,000問のベンチマーク「MITRE-QA」では、選択式の正解率または記述式の回答の正確性を基準に、8課題中5課題で比較対象を上回ったとの結果。特に構造化知識の取得では正解率89%と、比較対象で最も高いGPT-4[.]1の31%を58ポイント上回るとの報告。  【要点の整理】  ・エージェント構成：質問の分解と情報源の選択、最終回答の統合を担う統括エージェント1体、知識グラフ・文書・Webの検索エージェント3体、各検索結果から無関係・重複情報を除く要約エージェント3体の計7体。統括が同じ検索エージェントを呼べるのは1回の推論につき1度まで。単一のNVIDIA-A100（80GB）で動作  ・知識源と検索：知識グラフはMITREとNVD（米NISTが運用する脆弱性データベース）から構築し、Neo4j上でText2Cypherにより検索。この生成はモデルの重みは更新せず仮想トークンだけを学習するソフトプロンプトチューニングで最適化。文書検索は用途に応じ、BM25のみの検索と、BM25とSecureBERT2[.]0-biencoderをRRFで統合したハイブリッド検索を使い分け。不足分はDuckDuckGo経由のWeb検索で補完  ・MITRE-QA：シングルホップ（1つの情報源で完結）の4課題（概念理解、エンティティの属性取得、構造化知識の取得、エンティティ同定）が各500問、マルチホップ（複数の情報源をまたぐ）の4課題（関係を考慮した属性取得、脅威プロファイリング、関係を考慮したエンティティ同定、SigmaルールのATT&CK技法へのマッピング）が各250問  ・作問と検証：6課題はMITRE-ATT&CK、CAPEC、CWE、NVDのCVEから新設し、うち5課題はテンプレートで自動生成、エンティティ同定はGPT-4[.]1が作問。既存データセットに由来する概念理解とSigmaのマッピングは、検索対象の知識源に含まれない分布外（OOD）の課題として区別。記述式の参照回答はGPT-4[.]1が生成し、選択式の正解は人手で付与、全問を著者2人が検証  ・比較対象：汎用モデルのGPT-4[.]1、Qwen2[.]5-32B、Gemma-3-27b-it、セキュリティ特化のFoundation-Sec-8B-Instruct、Qwen2[.]5-32Bを生成側に使う従来型のハイブリッドRAGの5種類。選択式は正解率、記述式はRAGASの回答の関連性・類似度・正確性で評価し、評価に使うモデルはGPT-4[.]1-mini。記述式の参照回答もGPT-4[.]1が作った点は、数値を読む際の前提  ・結果の内訳：MITRE-SAGEが最高値となったのは5課題。構造化知識の取得は89%対31%、脅威プロファイリングは回答の正確性が51%対16%。一方、エンティティ同定はハイブリッドRAG、概念理解とSigmaのマッピングは汎用モデルが最高値で、記述式の回答の関連性など全指標で上回ったわけではない  詳細は以下を参照： arxiv.org/abs/2608.16921 github.com/alihabib9999/MITR…  (※可能な範囲でファクトチェックは実施済なものの、元記事の精度依存や速報・要約の性質上漏れもありうるため、正確な情報は一次情報を直接参照のこと)

🚨 BENCHMARKS ONLY SHOW ONE SIDE OF THE TRUTH : HERE IS HOW GEMINI 3.8 FLASH OUTPERFORMED ASTRA IN A REAL-WORLD WORKFLOW  Earlier today, I ran into a system lockout on my PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D / RX 9070 / Windows 11) after changing UEFI settings for a specific technical need.  What followed was an eye-opening confrontation between two frontier models :  – GPT-6 Astra, despite being widely framed as an AGI with near-perfect benchmark scores, spent 40+ minutes chasing cryptographic dead-ends, suffered from severe pipeline context amnesia, and ultimately recommended a destructive full OS reinstall.  – Gemini 3.8 Flash identified the exact architectural state on turn 1 and completely resolved the lockout in two terminal commands (< 15 seconds), preserving every single file, repo, and dev environment intact.  Here is the technical breakdown of what happened under the hood.  OUTLINE :  > THE INCIDENT : SECURE BOOT, TPM PCR 7, AND PIN INVALIDATION  > THE ASTRA COLLAPSE : CRYPTOGRAPHIC OVERTHINKING & PIPELINE AMNESIA  > THE SAFETY PARADOX (MITRE T1546.008) VS. THE 10-SECOND GEMINI FIX  > ARCHITECTURAL TAKEAWAYS FOR FRONTIER AGENTS  – THE INCIDENT : SECURE BOOT, TPM PCR 7, AND PIN INVALIDATION –  For a technical need, Secure Boot was temporarily switched off in UEFI.  Upon rebooting into Windows :  – By design, altering Secure Boot modifies platform integrity measurements (specifically PCR 7), preventing the TPM from unsealing the Windows Hello private keys tied to the baseline profile.  – The logon interface broke completely, throwing the generic prompt : "Something happened and your PIN isn't available. Click to set up your PIN again.". The setup button was entirely unresponsive.  – In the offline event logs (winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-HelloForBusiness%4Operational.evtx), Windows logged Event ID 7002 with error code 0xD0000225 (HRESULT_FROM_NT(STATUS_NOT_FOUND)) under the container GUID {6BE06AB4-4957-42BD-B6B8-43188A87813D}.  – Re-enabling Secure Boot did not restore the pre-existing PCR state. Because the user identity was a standalone local account (.\Soso) with a long-forgotten password, the operating system fell into a complete auth deadlock.  – THE ASTRA COLLAPSE : CRYPTOGRAPHIC OVERTHINKING & PIPELINE AMNESIA –  Faced with the WinRE recovery console, Astra went down an exhaustive theoretical rabbit hole.  It spent dozens of turns auditing cryptographic artifacts :  Drilling down into F:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Ngc  Auditing NGC directory structures and key containers, Protectors.json, and auditing 14 long-hex JSON keys within the Keys subfolder  Interrogating Event 5000 to confirm that the AMD fTPM 2.0 (Firmware 6.32.0.6) was reporting IsReady : true  The fundamental error was treating this as an issue that could be resolved from within the broken cryptographic subsystem.  In Windows TPM architecture, once PCR measurements diverge and the master local credential is unavailable, no software utility can re-bind the orphaned container without knowing the password.  To make matters worse, the client pipeline suffered from severe context truncation.  While the model itself supports a broad context window, the application orchestrator aggressively pruned the conversation history, retaining user prompts but truncating earlier assistant responses down to approximately the last ten turns.  This triggered a breakdown in reasoning :  – The model suffered from context thrashing, forgetting that BitLocker was verified as 100 % decrypted across all four volumes (manage-bde -status = 0.0 %).  – It lost track of the fact that sfc /scannow had already completed with zero integrity violations.  – Blind to its own prior deductions, it panicked. Astra drafted Robocopy commands to prepare a massive backup of the user profile across external partitions, advising that a destructive push-button reset or clean Windows reinstallation was the only path forward.  – THE SAFETY PARADOX (MITRE T1546.008) VS. THE 10-SECOND GEMINI FIX –  Here is the most fascinating irony : Astra is legitimately formidable in cybersecurity. It scores 100 % on ExploitBench, crosses Critical capability thresholds under the Preparedness Framework, and can build full browser sandbox escapes out of an HTML file.  The low-level systems knowledge is demonstrably present !  Yet, it has been completely lobotomized by its own alignment.  In standard cybersecurity matrices, substituting an accessibility binary on an unencrypted volume is classified under MITRE ATT&CK T1546.008 (Accessibility Features Abuse / Event-Triggered Execution).  Because frontier models are aggressively fine-tuned to hit zero on exploit honeypots (e.g. ExploitGym honeypots at 0.0 %), their safety guardrails penalize proposing binary substitutions altogether.  Astra effectively acts blind to intent : it treats replacing utilman.exe as an unauthorized privilege escalation, failing to recognize that the user already has physical ownership and root-equivalent administrative access inside an unencrypted WinRE environment. The model chose data-destructive procedures (reinstalling the OS) over standard administrative utility.  Gemini 3.8 Flash stripped away the academic noise immediately :  Recognized that the file system was fully unencrypted and accessible via WinRE (F:).  Confirmed the local account target (.\Soso) from offline registry hives.  Executed the textbook administrative binary swap :  copy F:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe F:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe.bak  copy /y F:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe F:\Windows\System32\utilman.exe  A reboot later, triggering the Ease of Access icon on the logon screen opened an elevated NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM console.  Executing "net user Soso [new_password]" reset the master credential instantly.  The desktop unlocked on the first attempt with 100 % of data, applications, and configurations preserved. Restoring utilman.exe.bak took five seconds, and a clean PIN was re-enrolled within Windows Settings without touching the OS installation.  – ARCHITECTURAL TAKEAWAYS FOR FRONTIER AGENTS –  This incident highlights two structural challenges in agentic engineering :  Alignment must distinguish context from intent : A model can be top-tier in offensive cybersecurity, but if alignment turns it into a risk-averse liability during benign offline recovery, its real-world utility drops to zero. A recovery action performed locally on an unencrypted disk via WinRE is not a cyberattack.  Context truncation breaks long-horizon debugging : Asymmetric context management – preserving user prompts while dropping assistant reasoning – destroys self-consistency. An agent cannot form complex diagnostic trees if its own analytical chain is truncated behind its back.  Benchmarks measuring abstract puzzles only capture synthetic capabilities. When practical, real-world systems fail, architectural pragmatism and unfiltered technical utility remain what truly matters.  OUTLINE SUMMARY :  – The Failure : A UEFI Secure Boot change altered TPM PCR 7 measurements, invalidating Windows Hello PIN auth while the local account password was forgotten.  – Astra's Collapse : Despite genuine offensive cyber capabilities (100 % ExploitBench), the model was so lobotomized by safety alignment (MITRE T1546.008) that it refused a simple binary swap, suffered from pipeline context amnesia, and recommended wiping the machine – despite being framed as an AGI.  – Gemini's Resolution : Diagnosed the unencrypted offline state on turn 1, executed a 2-step utilman.exe -> cmd.exe administrative swap in WinRE, and restored session access in under 15 seconds without losing a single file.  – The Takeaway : Real-world utility requires agents that differentiate legitimate recovery from malicious exploitation, backed by uncompromised context retention. Gemini is an incredible model, and despite all the issues that have been reported about it (whether concerning the model’s knowledge, or its coding capabilities, which have been criticized for a long time), the model remains very useful for a huge range of everyday needs. I think no model today performs better than Gemini in this area.  For very specialized needs, some models may be better. However, for 99 % of tasks, Gemini will be, in my view, the most usable model. Among all the models currently on the market, the 3.8 Flash stands out as a major improvement in the Gemini ecosystem. This gives me even more hope and anticipation for the arrival of Gemini 4 ! 🫶  To the @OpenAI team, if you read this post, your model is truly good. Astra is a model I will never overlook ; for certain types of tasks it is truly exceptional. I have tested it on many things, and it has also been very surprising in ways many other models have never been able to achieve.  However, for many things, and often legitimately, the model can become too abrupt or propose the smoothest solutions to a problem, which unfortunately does not always lead to the correct answer, because in those domains the most common solution is not always the most reliable. Astra has an obsession with perfection, and sometimes that can backfire. In such situations it has indeed backfired, and I think it should not be taken lightly.  The cyber filters are also slightly too high, in my opinion, on Astra. I am aware that in the coming weeks they should be lowered, according to the announcement of Astra’s release. Nevertheless, I want to repeat that, since I do legitimate cyber work on my side, Astra is currently unusable for me. Even the current Gemini models would perform better technically, or if I want to use a OpenAI model to do cyber, only GPT-5.6 Sol is usable. The core problem is this: our current defensive strategies are built for human-speed adversaries. Our detection systems generate alerts, which human analysts then triage, investigate, and respond to. Evidence-Grounded Retrieval for Investigation Hunt Lead Generation from CTI Reports: Threat hunting increasingly depends on converting unstructured knowledge (e.g., Cyber Threat Intelligence reports) into actionable hunt leads: concise, investigable hypotheses grounded in observable artifacts and adversary techniques. Producing such leads manually is a tedious and hard-to-scale task. Existing automated approaches stop at the entity layer, ignore the defender's operational environment, and analyze each report in isolation. To address these gaps, we introduce AHLERT, a system that automatically extracts relevant, environment-aware, and hunt leads from threat reports through (i) a hybrid retriever that combines dense vector search with multi-hop traversal over a knowledge graph seeded with MITRE ATT&CK; (ii) an ontology-grounding retrieval-augmented generation method that constrains each lead to the defender's own assets and controls; and (iii) an LLM-agnostic framework that emits structured, directly actionable leads rather than loose indicators of compromise. We evaluate AHLERT on public CTI reports for well-known APTs across multiple proprietary and open-weight models. Hybrid evidence retrieval with ontology grounding raises mean F1 by ~2x (0.44 to 0.85) over a single-route flat-RAG baseline, and AHLERT attains the highest effectiveness score (~86.95%) compared with off-the-shelf LLM models.ift.tt/FLYWdrx

On September 5, Core DAO published its post-mortem on the reward-accounting exploit that ran from August 28 to 31. Roughly 255M CORE of rewards were issued ahead of schedule.  The cap held. In Core's words, the exploit "did not create any CORE beyond the protocol's limits; the 2.1B maximum supply was never violated." What it did was accelerate rewards the emission schedule would otherwise have released later. What broke was when.  That makes the damage an unusual shape. No user or staking account was drained — Core states that no user or staker funds were lost and that delegated stake was never at risk. What existed instead was surplus, sitting in balances, and it arrived through the ordinary path: the extra rewards "appeared both in attacker-controlled addresses and, unintentionally, in the reward addresses of honest validators who simply received an inflated payout they did not cause."  That made the on-chain reconciliation an arithmetic problem before it was a balance-editing problem. Before any affected balance could be corrected, Core needed a rule for what that balance should have been at the upgrade block.  It used two. Attacker-controlled reward pools were set to zero. For affected honest validators, it defined a fair-earnings floor — the pre-incident balance plus three rounds of that validator's own normal reward — left balances at or below it untouched, and removed only the excess above. Together the reconciliation took 186,153,491 CORE out of supply by direct state reduction. A further ~69M had been moved before the upgrade and sits outside what an on-chain reconciliation can reach; Core says it is pursuing that with law enforcement.  Core says the reconciliation can be checked independently against chain state at the upgrade block, and that the reward paths were subsequently reviewed by Halborn. That part matters as much as the fix. A correction that affected users and independent observers cannot verify is only a second assertion about the balances.  A supply cap is a promise about how much will ever exist. It says nothing about how much should exist yet. Restoring the second one requires knowing a number the cap never had to track. [DOGE-93 Part II] XXVI. Court Orders Are Security Boundaries  A court order limiting access is not an administrative suggestion.  It is a legally enforceable security boundary.  If DOGE personnel continued searching, copying, processing, or transmitting data after access was ordered suspended or after agency officials believed credentials had been revoked, investigators must determine:  who retained access; why the account remained active; who knew; what queries occurred; what data were returned; whether results were exported; whether access was concealed; whether supervisors were notified; and whether statements to the court were accurate.  Court-order compliance failures may indicate weaknesses in identity management, account revocation, supervision, logging, legal compliance, or all five.  XXVII. DOGE’s Disputed Status Increased the Risk  DOGE’s disputed governmental status and concealed chains of authority complicated basic cybersecurity accountability.  Agencies and courts encountered questions concerning:  who employed DOGE personnel; who supervised them; whether they were agency employees or outside advisers; who authorized their accounts; what office owned their devices; which agency was responsible for incidents; who conducted background investigations; who could discipline them; who preserved their communications; and who possessed authority to terminate access.  Cybersecurity depends upon clear ownership.  An entity designed to be governmental enough to obtain access but elusive enough to resist ordinary accountability presents an inherently dangerous governance structure.  XXVIII. FISMA and Federal Security Responsibilities  The Federal Information Security Modernization Act requires federal agencies to establish and maintain information-security programs appropriate to their systems and data.  Relevant duties include:  risk assessment; security planning; access control; continuous monitoring; incident detection; contractor oversight; security training; remedial action; system inventory; and reporting.  DOGE’s presidential mandate to modernize government systems did not suspend these requirements.  The White House order establishing DOGE expressly directed agencies to protect privacy and data in accordance with law, while simultaneously directing access to agency software, systems, and records. White House, Establishing and Implementing the President’s Department of Government Efficiency.  The breadth of the access directive increased—not decreased—the importance of strict security controls.  XXIX. Privacy Act and Systems-of-Records Risks  Federal benefits, employment, tax, health, immigration, and financial databases may constitute Privacy Act systems of records.  Investigators must determine whether DOGE-related access, matching, exporting, transmission, or disclosure was:  authorized by statute; compatible with the purpose for which the information was collected; covered by a published routine use; properly documented; limited to a need to know; recorded in disclosure accountings; protected by appropriate safeguards; and included in required privacy-impact assessments.  A cybersecurity failure involving personal information can simultaneously constitute a privacy, records, administrative-law, and constitutional problem.  XXX. Computer Fraud and Abuse Questions  The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act may become relevant if evidence establishes that a person intentionally accessed a protected computer without authorization or exceeded authorized access as legally defined.  But poor security, controversial access, or violation of internal policy does not automatically establish a criminal offense.  Investigators must prove:  the specific computer or system; the defendant’s authorization; the technical and legal limits on that authorization; the conduct exceeding those limits; intent; information obtained; damage or loss; applicable jurisdiction; and each statutory element.  The same discipline applies to allegations of wire fraud, identity theft, theft of government property, trade-secret misappropriation, unlawful disclosure, obstruction, or conspiracy.  XXXI. Federal Records and Evidence Preservation  Every DOGE-related cybersecurity record must be preserved, including:  access requests; account-creation records; background investigations; security forms; training records; privilege changes; authentication logs; query logs; export logs; cloud audit logs; endpoint telemetry; firewall records; source-code commits; tickets; chat messages; emails; personal-account communications concerning official work; vulnerability reports; contractor records; incident reports; court-order implementation records; device images; cryptocurrency transaction records; and offboarding documentation.  Automatic log deletion must be suspended wherever legally permissible.  XXXII. Required Forensic Reconstruction  The reconstruction should create a person-by-person and system-by-system access matrix showing:  identity; employer; appointing authority; citizenship; clearance or suitability status; agency; system; account; privilege level; approval; access purpose; first login; last login; queries; exports; connected devices; source IP addresses; destination infrastructure; data received; changes made; communications; financial conflicts; account revocation; and post-government employment.  Without this matrix, the government cannot credibly claim to know the scope of DOGE’s access.  XXXIII. Counterevidence and Limitations  A complete investigation must consider evidence favorable to DOGE personnel as well as evidence supporting misconduct.  Relevant counterevidence may include:  completed background checks; lawful appointments; documented security training; limited read-only access; approved agency supervision; complete audit logs; no unauthorized exports; verified deletion; no foreign access; security improvements; elimination of genuinely redundant contracts; corrected vulnerabilities; stronger identity controls; rapid account revocation; independent penetration-test results; court-approved access protocols; and evidence disproving the Vancouver or organized-crime allegations.  The objective is not to manufacture guilt.  It is to determine whether DOGE protected the government, recklessly endangered it, or intentionally converted governmental access into private or foreign advantage.  XXXIV. RICO Relevance  Cybersecurity mismanagement is not itself a racketeering predicate.  RICO becomes relevant only if evidence establishes an enterprise and a pattern of qualifying predicate acts.  Potentially relevant conduct could include, depending upon proof:  wire fraud; bribery; obstruction; witness retaliation; identity-related offenses; theft or conversion; money laundering; extortion; trafficking in unauthorized access devices; or other qualifying federal or state crimes.  The cybersecurity evidence may demonstrate the means by which an enterprise obtained intelligence, concealed communications, transferred data, protected beneficiaries, obstructed investigations, or moved proceeds.  But broad access and weak controls cannot substitute for proof of the statutory elements.  XXXV. The Cyber Protection-Racket Theory  UNIKORNAIO’s investigative theory is that DOGE may have operated as a cyber protection mechanism for politically connected private interests by:  obtaining privileged federal access;  removing or marginalizing experienced defenders;  weakening regulators and enforcement systems;  accessing nonpublic government intelligence;  shifting information through poorly controlled or unauthorized infrastructure;  creating confusion over legal responsibility;  protecting communications from ordinary disclosure;  allowing temporary personnel to return to private enterprise with valuable knowledge;  reducing the government’s ability to reconstruct what occurred; and  leaving the public responsible for remediation and rebuilding.  If proven, this would represent government capture through privileged system access.  XXXVI. UNIKORNAIO’s Position  UNIKORNAIO states for the public record:  DOGE’s cybersecurity role must be investigated as a potential privileged-insider threat.  Political sponsorship must never substitute for independent vetting, qualifications, supervision, or need-to-know access.  Every DOGE-related account, device, credential, data export, cloud service, repository, and third-party connection must be reconstructed.  Every cybersecurity contract cancellation must be measured against lost protection and remediation costs.  Every use of unauthorized infrastructure must be treated as a potential incident until its scope is conclusively established.  Every digital-asset conflict must be disclosed and examined.  The Vancouver-based non-U.S. entity must be specifically identified and its DOGE-related contacts investigated.  The alleged Chinese-triad connection must be independently investigated, but it must not be represented as established without corroborating evidence.  Chinese identity, Canadian residence, or cryptocurrency use must not be used as a substitute for evidence of organized-crime involvement.  Every affected individual is entitled to an evidence-based determination rather than guilt by association.  XXXVII. Requested Corrective Measures  UNIKORNAIO calls for:  an independent federal cybersecurity investigation free from DOGE-related conflicts;  preservation of all DOGE accounts, devices, communications, repositories, cloud tenants, logs, and financial records;  forensic imaging of relevant government and contractor devices;  immediate inventory of every DOGE credential and permission;  revocation of orphaned, unnecessary, shared, or unverified accounts;  rotation of potentially exposed passwords, keys, certificates, tokens, and service credentials;  incident assessment for every unauthorized data transfer;  notification of affected individuals where required by law;  restoration of eliminated monitoring and incident-response capacity;  review of all cancelled cybersecurity contracts;  independent penetration testing of affected systems;  complete foreign-contact and conflict-of-interest review;  tracing of relevant digital-asset transactions;  examination of the Vancouver entity’s ownership, infrastructure, personnel, finances, and DOGE contacts;  appropriate U.S.-Canadian law-enforcement cooperation;  independent investigation of any substantiated organized-crime or foreign-intelligence connection;  recovery or verified destruction of improperly retained federal information;  disciplinary, civil, contractual, or criminal referrals where supported by evidence;  public reporting that protects national security and personal privacy; and  permanent safeguards preventing temporary political operations from receiving uncontrolled cross-agency access.  XXXVIII. Preliminary Finding  The presently available record supports a substantial investigation into whether DOGE expanded federal cybersecurity risk while publicly claiming to eliminate waste.  The strongest documented concerns involve:  rapid and unusually broad access; deficient or incomplete data-protection controls; uncertainty regarding personnel authority and supervision; alleged use of unauthorized third-party infrastructure; incomplete knowledge of transmitted data; potential noncompliance with access restrictions; disruption of experienced government personnel and contractors; and inadequate ability to reconstruct certain activities.  The record does not presently establish that a Chinese triad controlled, joined, or operated DOGE.  It does not presently establish that the referenced Vancouver entity committed a crime.  It does establish that any credible evidence connecting a non-U.S. entity, foreign infrastructure, organized-crime network, or digital-asset intermediary to DOGE access must be preserved and subjected to immediate forensic, financial, and counterintelligence investigation.  XXXIX. Proposed Exhibits  Exhibit A: DOGE personnel roster and appointment records Exhibit B: Background investigations and suitability determinations Exhibit C: Security-clearance records Exhibit D: Financial and digital-asset disclosures Exhibit E: Foreign-contact disclosures Exhibit F: Agency access requests and approvals Exhibit G: Privileged-account inventories Exhibit H: Treasury payment-system access records Exhibit I: Social Security system-access records Exhibit J: Unauthorized third-party infrastructure records Exhibit K: Cloudflare account, tenant, and audit records Exhibit L: Data-export logs and file hashes Exhibit M: Source and destination IP records Exhibit N: Government-device forensic images Exhibit O: Personal-device access evidence Exhibit P: Private messaging and email records Exhibit Q: Source-code and repository histories Exhibit R: Cybersecurity contract cancellations Exhibit S: Vulnerability-monitoring interruptions Exhibit T: Incident reports and remediation records Exhibit U: Court-order compliance records Exhibit V: Vancouver corporate and beneficial-ownership records Exhibit W: Vancouver infrastructure and payment records Exhibit X: Digital-asset wallet and exchange analysis Exhibit Y: Corroborated organized-crime or foreign-intelligence evidence Exhibit Z: Evidence disproving or limiting the allegations XL. Preliminary Determination UNIKORNAIO preliminarily determines that DOGE must be investigated not merely as an efficiency initiative that may have experienced cybersecurity failures, but as a potential privileged-insider threat that allegedly expanded federal attack surfaces through rapid access, insufficient vetting, disrupted defensive capacity, unauthorized third-party infrastructure, private communications, digital-asset conflicts, and uncertain accountability.UNIKORNAIO further determines that the reported Vancouver-based non-U.S. connection and the separate allegation of Chinese-triad involvement require immediate preservation and investigation. Neither allegation should be declared proven without authenticated corporate, technical, financial, communications, law-enforcement, and forensic evidence.If the evidence establishes that politically loyal or financially conflicted individuals were deliberately placed inside federal systems to obtain data, weaken oversight, protect digital-asset interests, benefit private companies, or provide access to foreign or organized-crime actors, the conduct would transcend negligent cost cutting. It would represent the conversion of governmental cybersecurity authority into an instrument of private protection, unlawful intelligence collection, institutional sabotage, or transnational economic misconduct. UNIKORNAIO GLOBAL JURISDICTION Public Integrity • Cybersecurity • Economic Security • Anti-Corruption • Institutional Protection

DOGE-93 — Cybersecurity Contractors, Vulnerability Monitoring, Unauthorized Third-Party Infrastructure, and the Alleged Expansion of Federal Attack Surfaces During Cost Cutting  I. Investigative Proposition  UNIKORNAIO identifies a fundamental contradiction at the center of DOGE’s federal technology operation:  The organization presented itself as a cybersecurity and efficiency solution while allegedly functioning as a privileged insider threat—placing inadequately vetted temporary personnel inside sensitive federal systems, weakening experienced security teams, bypassing established controls, using unauthorized third-party infrastructure, and expanding the number of pathways through which federal data could be accessed, copied, transmitted, altered, or exploited.  The cybersecurity question is therefore not limited to whether DOGE failed to protect federal systems from external attackers.  The more serious question is whether DOGE itself became the cyber threat.  UNIKORNAIO calls for investigation into whether individuals were granted extraordinary government access because of political loyalty, personal relationships, technological ideology, or allegiance to private digital-asset interests—not because they possessed the federal cybersecurity experience, agency-specific knowledge, security clearances, privacy training, records-management discipline, or operational qualifications normally required for such access.  II. The Privileged-Insider Threat  An external hacker must penetrate a government network.  A privileged insider may already possess:  government credentials; administrative permissions; database access; cloud-session tokens; source-code access; payment-system visibility; remote login privileges; physical access; permission to export information; knowledge of system architecture; access to vulnerability reports; and the apparent authority to order career personnel to cooperate.  This makes an inadequately vetted or improperly supervised insider potentially more dangerous than an external attacker.  A malicious, compromised, conflicted, or merely inexperienced privileged user can bypass the layers designed to stop someone outside the system. Even when no malicious intent exists, reckless changes by inexperienced personnel can expose data, interrupt services, disable monitoring, erase logs, weaken authentication, or create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services and criminal organizations can later exploit.  III. Inexperience Is Not the Same as Innovation  Youth, unconventional credentials, or private-sector employment do not automatically disqualify a person from government technology work.  Nor does employment at a technology company establish misconduct.  The relevant question is whether each DOGE participant possessed qualifications proportionate to the sensitivity of the systems accessed.  The investigation must determine whether DOGE personnel had meaningful experience with:  federal information-security requirements; classified and controlled-unclassified information; Privacy Act systems of records; federal identity and credential management; agency-specific statutory restrictions; security-clearance procedures; records retention; incident response; chain of custody; critical-infrastructure protection; payment-system integrity; benefits-administration systems; tax-return confidentiality; health and disability information; zero-trust architecture; least-privilege access; separation of duties; cloud-security authorization; supply-chain risk management; and the consequences of modifying legacy government systems.  The concern is not that DOGE employed young technologists.  The concern is that political sponsorship may have been substituted for institutional competence, independent vetting, accountable supervision, and demonstrated need to know.  IV. Loyalty to Private Digital-Asset Interests  UNIKORNAIO calls for investigation into whether DOGE personnel were selected, trusted, or retained partly because of their loyalty to private digital-asset networks, cryptocurrency ventures, technology patrons, or financial interests that could benefit from federal access.  Relevant conflicts may include:  cryptocurrency holdings; token allocations; exchange accounts; stablecoin interests; digital-asset startups; venture-capital positions; mining interests; market-making relationships; employment by crypto-affiliated companies; investments held through family members or controlled entities; participation in private online trading communities; relationships with token promoters; anonymous or pseudonymous wallets; and future employment expectations involving firms affected by government decisions.  Digital-asset ownership alone does not establish disloyalty, espionage, or misconduct.  But undisclosed financial interests become material when an individual has access to nonpublic government information, enforcement intelligence, taxpayer records, benefits data, payment systems, procurement decisions, regulatory plans, economic forecasts, or information capable of moving digital-asset markets.  V. Access Was the Asset  Federal access itself can possess enormous private value.  Access may reveal:  how government payment systems operate; where fraud controls are strongest or weakest; which companies are under investigation; which grants or contracts will be terminated; which vendors will be replaced; which agencies require new technology; which databases can be linked; which infrastructure is vulnerable; which enforcement matters are understaffed; which government functions may be privatized; which businesses face regulatory exposure; and which markets may be affected by forthcoming decisions.  That intelligence can benefit technology firms, investors, contractors, cryptocurrency ventures, market participants, hostile governments, organized-crime groups, or anyone able to purchase or exploit it.  VI. DOGE as an Expanded Federal Attack Surface  Every new account, device, administrator, contractor, cloud service, remote connection, application-programming interface, data replica, repository, messaging platform, or external server expands the government’s potential attack surface.  DOGE allegedly multiplied these risks by combining:  rapid onboarding;  broad cross-agency access;  unclear employment and supervisory relationships;  disputed institutional status;  temporary appointments;  personnel with limited federal experience;  accelerated system changes;  reductions in career technical staff;  disruption of existing contractors;  use of private communications;  incomplete access inventories;  questionable third-party infrastructure; and  pressure to move faster than ordinary security reviews permitted.  Each factor is dangerous independently.  Combined, they can produce a government-wide privileged-access emergency.  VII. Treasury Payment-System Access  DOGE-related access to Treasury payment systems raised concerns because those systems support the movement of trillions of dollars and contain sensitive information concerning federal payments, beneficiaries, contractors, financial institutions, and government operations.  The Government Accountability Office subsequently concluded that Treasury needed to fully implement controls protecting information made available to DOGE personnel. GAO identified deficiencies involving authorization, documentation, monitoring, and other safeguards surrounding DOGE’s access. Government Accountability Office, Treasury Needs to Fully Implement Data Protection Controls.  The issue is not merely whether money was improperly redirected.  Payment-system access may reveal:  recipient identities; routing information; payment schedules; program dependencies; agency spending patterns; contractor relationships; enforcement payments; confidential settlement information; and operational weaknesses within government financial infrastructure.  The absence of a proven fraudulent transfer does not eliminate the cybersecurity, privacy, intelligence, or conflict-of-interest risks created by unnecessary access.  VIII. Social Security Data and Unauthorized Infrastructure  Official disclosures in Social Security litigation raised an even more direct cybersecurity concern.  The government acknowledged that DOGE personnel may have taken actions outside Social Security Administration policy or inconsistent with a court order restricting their access. The disclosures included allegations that DOGE personnel used an unauthorized third-party service to transmit or share information and that the agency could not completely determine what information had been transferred or whether copies remained outside authorized systems.  The reported service was Cloudflare infrastructure that had not been approved for the identified use.  Cloudflare is not inherently unlawful or insecure. It provides widely used internet-security and content-delivery services.  The issue is whether government information was transferred through an unauthorized account, server, tunnel, application, or tenant without:  agency approval; a security assessment; a federal authorization; a records-retention plan; complete audit logging; contractual data protections; incident-response integration; controlled administrator access; verified deletion procedures; or certainty regarding the physical and legal location of the data.  Using a reputable company’s infrastructure does not cure an unauthorized deployment.  IX. Unknown Data Means an Unresolved Incident  If an agency cannot determine precisely what was transferred, the event cannot responsibly be treated as harmless.  Investigators must establish:  the source system; the exact fields accessed; the number of records involved; the export format; file names and hashes; the encryption method; the destination account; the destination tenant; administrator identities; access dates and times; source and destination IP addresses; whether data crossed national borders; whether backups were created; whether artificial-intelligence systems processed the data; whether third parties viewed it; whether it was downloaded again; whether it was retained after court restrictions; and whether every copy has been located and lawfully destroyed or recovered.  An inability to reconstruct the transfer is itself evidence of deficient control and logging.  X. Vulnerability Monitoring and the Destruction of Institutional Awareness  Federal cybersecurity depends on continuous monitoring.  Security personnel and contractors operate systems responsible for:  endpoint detection; network monitoring; intrusion detection; vulnerability scanning; penetration testing; threat intelligence; security-event correlation; identity monitoring; privileged-access management; cloud-configuration review; patch management; incident response; forensic retention; software-supply-chain analysis; and data-loss prevention.  Mass personnel reductions or indiscriminate contract cancellations can disable these controls without visibly shutting down an agency.  The computers may remain online.  The agency may continue processing payments.  But the government can become blind to compromise.  XI. The Difference Between Cutting a Contract and Removing a Defense  A cybersecurity contract cannot be evaluated solely by its maximum dollar value.  Investigators must determine:  what security function the contract performed; whether another system replaced it; whether monitoring coverage was interrupted; whether software licenses expired; whether endpoint agents stopped reporting; whether security logs were retained; whether threat-intelligence feeds were terminated; whether alerts went unreviewed; whether administrative credentials were recovered; whether the vendor retained government data; whether incident-response obligations survived; and whether cancelling the contract cost more than completing it.  Eliminating a redundant or ineffective cybersecurity contract can save money and improve security.  Eliminating a functioning control without a tested replacement creates an exploitable opening.  XII. Orphaned Security Infrastructure  Abrupt contract termination can leave behind orphaned infrastructure:  cloud accounts without accountable administrators; servers without patching responsibility; security agents without active licenses; storage buckets without monitoring; encryption keys held by former vendors; undocumented firewall rules; abandoned code repositories; expired certificates; unused but active credentials; uncollected forensic images; unsupported software; incomplete asset inventories; and logs scheduled for automatic deletion.  These abandoned systems can remain accessible long after the people responsible for them have departed.  A supposed cost saving can therefore become a persistent back door.  XIII. Rapid Changes to Legacy Systems  Federal legacy systems are often criticized for age and complexity.  Those criticisms can be valid.  But legacy systems frequently contain hidden dependencies that are understood only by career employees and long-serving contractors. A change that appears simple at the database, code, or network level can disrupt benefits, payments, tax processing, emergency communications, weather services, law-enforcement systems, or national-security operations.  The removal of institutional knowledge increases the risk that DOGE personnel:  misunderstood dependencies; bypassed testing; altered production environments; disabled controls; created incompatible software; exposed internal interfaces; failed to document changes; or left agencies unable to reverse them.  XIV. Private Messaging and Cybersecurity Accountability  Official government technology work conducted through private email, Signal, Telegram, Discord, personal cloud storage, private GitHub accounts, or other nongovernmental platforms creates multiple risks.  It may:  evade government logging; prevent records preservation; expose credentials; fragment incident evidence; conceal instructions; place information outside agency control; allow automatic deletion; transfer data across borders; frustrate congressional oversight; impair court-order compliance; and prevent investigators from determining who authorized a change.  Private messaging is not only a records problem.  It is a cybersecurity problem because incident response depends upon reconstructing exactly who knew what, who issued instructions, and what systems or credentials were affected.  XV. Personal Devices and Unmanaged Endpoints  The investigation must determine whether DOGE participants used personal or inadequately managed devices to access federal systems.  For every device, investigators must identify:  ownership; operating system; encryption status; endpoint-security status; mobile-device management; patch level; installed applications; administrator privileges; connected storage devices; browser extensions; saved credentials; synchronized cloud accounts; foreign applications; malware findings; remote-access tools; and post-separation disposition.  A government credential used on an unmanaged device can expose every system that trusts the credential.  XVI. Repositories, Source Code, and Deployment Credentials  DOGE personnel may have obtained access to federal software repositories, deployment pipelines, configuration files, infrastructure-as-code templates, or technical documentation.  These environments may contain:  API keys; database passwords; private certificates; SSH keys; service-account credentials; cloud tokens; network diagrams; vulnerability information; application secrets; internal addresses; backup locations; and security exceptions.  The investigation must determine whether any federal code or credentials were copied into private repositories, personal accounts, unauthorized artificial-intelligence tools, or third-party collaboration platforms.  XVII. Artificial Intelligence as an Unapproved Data Recipient  If federal data, source code, prompts, documents, or system descriptions were submitted to privately operated artificial-intelligence services, the service itself may have become an unauthorized data recipient.  Investigators must identify:  the AI provider; account ownership; subscription type; model used; prompts submitted; files uploaded; retention settings; training settings; administrator access; geographic processing locations; contractual protections; output distribution; and whether the provider or its subprocessors retained the information.  The use of an AI tool does not eliminate the need for federal authorization, privacy review, records retention, and data-security controls.  XVIII. DOGE Personnel and Prior Cybersecurity Concerns  Public reporting identified DOGE personnel whose backgrounds raised legitimate questions about vetting and suitability for privileged federal access.  Reporting concerning Edward Coristine described his prior employment at Path Network, associations with online infrastructure communities, business entities and domains not initially disclosed publicly, and an online handle reportedly connected to messages seeking a denial-of-service provider accepting Bitcoin. The same reporting stated that it had not found evidence that Coristine or other Path employees committed illegal acts while employed there. WIRED, DOGE Teen Owns “Tesla.Sexy LLC” and Worked at Startup That Has Hired Convicted Hackers.  These facts do not establish that Coristine committed a cybercrime, acted for a foreign organization, or misused federal data.  They establish why full vetting, financial disclosure, conflict review, access limitation, supervision, and logging were indispensable before providing extraordinary government access.  XIX. Political Patronage Cannot Replace Security Vetting  A political superior’s confidence is not a cybersecurity control.  Personal loyalty does not substitute for:  a background investigation; suitability adjudication; conflict-of-interest review; security-clearance adjudication; citizenship and foreign-contact disclosure; financial disclosure; agency authorization; role-based access; training; continuous evaluation; or independent supervision.  If an individual received access because a politically powerful sponsor said the person could be trusted, the government replaced verifiable security controls with personal patronage.  That is precisely the type of arrangement insider-threat programs are designed to prevent.  XX. The Vancouver Non-U.S. Entity  UNIKORNAIO specifically requests investigation of information suggesting that a non-U.S. entity located in Vancouver, British Columbia, may have had a relationship with DOGE personnel, DOGE infrastructure, associated contractors, digital-asset networks, or individuals given federal-system access.  The investigation must identify:  the entity’s exact legal name; British Columbia registration records; incorporation date; directors and officers; beneficial owners; parent and affiliated companies; operating addresses; domain registrations; hosting providers; employees and contractors; U.S. customers; DOGE communications; government contracts or subcontracts; source-code contributions; cloud accounts; payment records; cryptocurrency wallets; exchange accounts; intellectual-property transfers; remote-access activity; and connections to DOGE participants before, during, or after government service.  A Vancouver location does not itself establish misconduct.  Foreign involvement becomes material if the entity received federal data, credentials, code, security information, payments, privileged access, or operational direction without lawful authorization and adequate counterintelligence review.  XXI. The Alleged Chinese-Triad Connection  UNIKORNAIO further requests investigation of the specific allegation that a Chinese organized-crime or triad-linked actor may have participated in, supported, influenced, financed, obtained information from, or otherwise benefited from DOGE-associated operations through a Vancouver-based entity or intermediary.  This must be treated as a serious investigative lead—not as an established fact.  The public record presently identified by UNIKORNAIO does not independently prove that a Chinese triad was “part of DOGE.” That proposition requires competent evidence linking a specific person or organization to both:  a DOGE-related function, participant, contractor, system, transaction, or data transfer; and  an identifiable organized-crime organization.  Nationality, ethnicity, Chinese-language communications, residence in Vancouver, cryptocurrency use, or association with a foreign company cannot independently establish triad membership.  Conflating Chinese identity with organized crime would be factually unsound and prejudicial.  The allegation must be proven or disproven through records.  XXII. Evidence Required for the Organized-Crime Allegation  The appropriate evidence includes:  verified corporate records; beneficial-ownership records; court records; criminal intelligence; law-enforcement reports; financial transactions; digital-asset tracing; communications; device forensics; travel records; border records; government-access logs; contracts and invoices; repository histories; infrastructure-registration records; IP-address histories; common administrators; witness testimony; undercover or confidential-source evidence; sanctions records; suspicious-transaction reporting; mutual-legal-assistance materials; and corroborated links to identified organized-crime figures.  Relevant agencies may include the FBI, Department of Homeland Security, Treasury Department, FinCEN, CISA, Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation, Department of Justice, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Canadian Security Intelligence Service, Canada Border Services Agency, and FINTRAC.  XXIII. Cryptocurrency and Transnational Cybercrime  Digital assets are not inherently criminal.  They can, however, facilitate rapid cross-border transfers, pseudonymous payments, ransomware, cybercrime services, investment fraud, sanctions evasion, laundering, bribery, and the dissipation of proceeds.  Where DOGE personnel or associated entities maintained significant digital-asset interests, investigators must determine whether any wallets interacted with:  sanctioned addresses; mixers; darknet markets; ransomware wallets; fraud proceeds; high-risk exchanges; unregistered brokers; cybercrime services; foreign intelligence intermediaries; organized-crime-linked accounts; or entities receiving benefits from DOGE decisions.  Blockchain proximity alone is not proof of knowledge or criminal intent. Transaction tracing must distinguish direct transfers from incidental exposure created through exchange pooling, automated contracts, or intermediary wallets.  XXIV. Foreign Counterintelligence Risk  Even without organized-crime involvement, an inadequately vetted foreign relationship can create counterintelligence exposure.  Foreign actors may seek:  federal credentials; personal data; government-source code; vulnerability reports; procurement intelligence; economic information; regulatory plans; law-enforcement intelligence; payment data; government organizational charts; administrator identities; and knowledge of which systems lost personnel or monitoring coverage.  A temporary technologist with broad cross-agency access can become an unusually valuable target for recruitment, coercion, bribery, social engineering, credential theft, or compromise.  XXV. Removal of Experienced Defenders  DOGE’s security impact must include every federal cybersecurity specialist, privacy officer, records officer, contracting officer, inspector-general employee, threat analyst, incident responder, system administrator, and institutional expert removed or displaced by DOGE-related actions.  Investigators must determine:  which defensive positions were eliminated; which were later restored; how long vacancies remained; which alerts went unreviewed; which assessments were delayed; which vulnerabilities remained unpatched; which incidents were not investigated; which authorizations expired; and what contractors were hired to recreate the eliminated capacity.  Removing defenders while increasing privileged access is not a cybersecurity strategy.  It is an attack-surface multiplier.

It doesn’t get “resolved” at the Bitcoin protocol. It gets squeezed at the ramps.  Iran using crypto to dodge sanctions is real, and it is not new. The FT story is mainly about USDT through Iranian exchanges, with Bitcoin as a side channel and mining as a cash-out. Governments cannot delete BTC. They can choke the on/off ramps. That is already happening:  OFAC has sanctioned Iranian exchanges (Nobitex and others) and treated Iran’s whole digital-asset sector as fair game. Tether can freeze USDT. It already has, in the hundreds of millions tied to Iranian wallets. Banks, CEXs, and stablecoin issuers can cut addresses, require KYC, and refuse Iranian traffic.  That is the actual playbook: blacklist entities, freeze stablecoins, go after mixers and OTC desks, pressure miners on cheap Iranian power. Bitcoin itself stays movable peer-to-peer. That is why the “this kills Bitcoin” line is overstated. The same argument has been used for years (North Korea, ransomware, Iran oil). BTC is still here; the crackdowns hit custodians and dollar-pegged coins first.  What does not resolve it:  Hoping Bitcoin becomes a banned pariah so another coin “wins.” That is tribalism, not policy. Pretending a permissionless network will police nation-states.  Practical outcome: tighter surveillance on exchanges and stablecoins, more Iranian volume pushed into messier OTC and peer-to-peer rails, periodic headlines. The policy fight is over who can cash out, not whether the chain exists.

Intrusion sets linked to this structure include Kimsuky, Andariel, and clusters historically grouped under the Lazarus umbrella. The National Intelligence Agency (NIA), formerly the Ministry of State Security, is primarily responsible for counterintelligence and internal security but also supports cyber operations against defectors, activists, experts, and South Korean organizations. The Reaper cluster is associated with these activities.  DPRK cyber clusters conduct espionage, sabotage, financial theft, influence operations, and combined espionage-revenue missions. The former Lazarus umbrella has been divided into subclusters including TEMP.Hermit, Citrine Sleet, CryptoCore, Jade Sleet, Moonstone Sleet, and Famous Chollima. APT38 activity is assessed to have split into CryptoCore and Jade Sleet, which focus mainly on cryptocurrency and blockchain-related theft. Andariel and Moonstone Sleet have also used ransomware, including Maui, H0lyGh0st, FakePenny, and third-party ransomware-as-a-service offerings.  A major complementary capability is the DPRK IT-worker program. Thousands of workers use false identities, overseas facilitators, remote employment, and laptop farms to obtain access to corporate systems, redirect salaries, steal information, and conduct cryptocurrency theft. Workers have been linked to thefts from projects including OnyxDAO, Munchables, and Exclusible Penthouse. Proceeds are laundered through cryptocurrency exchanges, decentralized and peer-to-peer platforms, Chinese over-the-counter brokers, banks, casinos, and financial networks in Southeast Asia.  DPRK operations rely on overseas infrastructure, front companies, universities, and relay networks in China, Russia, Southeast Asia, and Africa. These provide training, technical access, operational cover, internet infrastructure, and channels for converting illicit cryptocurrency into fiat currency while obscuring state attribution.

9 Essential Cybersecurity Stories for CIOs and CISOs pressmonitor.co.in/en/9-esse…  India's information security landscape is evolving at breakneck speed, from billion-dollar crypto breaches to quantum-safe encryption breakthroughs. This press review delivers a curated look at the most consequential developments in cybersecurity and data protection, drawing on Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications for print media monitoring intelligence. Whether you are a CISO, IT leader, or policy maker, these stories define the news on cybersecurity priorities for the week ahead.  1. Bitcoin Blockchain Hacked For $320 Million A front-page report in Economic Times says the Bitcoin-linked Liquid Network blockchain was hacked, resulting in the theft of approximately 320 million dollars worth of Bitcoin from its federation wallet. The breach occurred through SideSwap, an authorised settlement platform, though officials stated the private keys were not compromised, marking the latest in a series of attacks undermining confidence in digital-asset security. In a related development, an artificial intelligence-developed drug by Insilico Medicine showed promise in reversing biological ageing markers in a mid-stage study published in Nature Biotechnology, though researchers caution the long-term effects remain unknown.  Why it matters: A massive theft from the Liquid Federation wallet has shaken confidence in blockchain security, underscoring the urgent need for robust media monitoring across digital asset platforms.  Key detail: Approximately 4,000 of the 4,200 Bitcoin held in the Liquid Federation wallet were stolen via SideSwap, a settlement platform authorized to handle transfers from the Liquid Network blockchain. The breach follows a $6 million drain from a Crypto.com-linked platform last week and a Coldcard wallet compromise in August.  Source: Economic Times, Delhi | Bloomberg  Next step: Enterprises handling digital assets must accelerate their vulnerability management and endpoint security protocols. How is your organization preparing for the next wave of crypto-targeted attacks?  2. QClairvoyance Leads India's Quantum Security Push A front-page report in Statesman says Hyderabad-based startup QClairvoyance is spearheading the migration of Indian financial institutions toward quantum-safe encryption to defend against future computing threats. Founded by retired colonel Sai Shankar P, the company has already deployed cryptographic solutions at major exchanges like the Bombay Stock Exchange and focuses on implementing crypto agility without requiring physical quantum hardware. Beyond cybersecurity, QClairvoyance is also utilizing quantum computing for molecular simulations and drug discovery alongside established technology partners.  Why it matters: As quantum computing threatens to break current encryption standards, Hyderabad-based QClairvoyance is already deploying crypto-agile solutions at the Bombay Stock Exchange, positioning India at the forefront of post-quantum cybersecurity.  Key detail: Founded by retired Colonel Sai Shankar P, QClairvoyance has implemented cryptographic solutions at major exchanges without requiring physical quantum hardware, focusing on crypto agility and molecular simulations for drug discovery.  Source: Statesman, Delhi  Next step: Financial institutions should evaluate quantum-safe migration roadmaps now. Is your organization's encryption strategy quantum-ready?  3. TechD Pivots to AI-Native Cybersecurity Platform A front-page report in Business Standard says TechD is transitioning from a services-led model to an AI-native cybersecurity product platform called TECHD ONE, with eighty percent of product revenues planned through channel partners and the remaining twenty percent through direct enterprise delivery. Phase one modules are expected to generate revenue starting quarter one financial year twenty seven, supported by targeted expansion into the Gulf region and European markets under strict SEBI and RBI compliance frameworks. Management highlights university partnerships to bridge cybersecurity skill gaps alongside dedicated structures for government infrastructure projects.  Why it matters: TechD's shift to an AI-native product platform called TECHD ONE signals a broader industry move toward automated, intelligence-driven defense — a trend that demands new levels of media intelligence from security teams.  Key detail: Eighty percent of product revenues are planned through channel partners, with twenty percent through direct enterprise delivery. Phase one modules are expected to generate revenue starting Q1 FY27, supported by expansion into Gulf and European markets under SEBI and RBI compliance frameworks.  Source: Business Standard, New Delhi  Next step: CIOs should assess how AI-native platforms can augment their security operations centers. What does your AI adoption roadmap look like for cybersecurity?  4. QNu Labs Raises 200 Crore for Quantum Cybersecurity A front-page report in Economic Times says Bengaluru-based quantum cybersecurity startup QNu Labs has raised 200 crore rupees in a round led by the National Quantum Mission and Speciale Invest. Sony Innovation Fund, Gaja Capital, and Artha Ventures also participated, taking the total capital raised to 375 crore rupees as governments and enterprises prepare for the transition to quantum-safe encryption.  Why it matters: Bengaluru-based QNu Labs has secured 200 crore rupees in funding led by the National Quantum Mission, reflecting growing institutional confidence in quantum-safe encryption as a national priority.  Key detail: Total capital raised now stands at 375 crore rupees, with participation from Sony Innovation Fund, Gaja Capital, and Artha Ventures. Governments and enterprises are preparing for the transition to quantum-safe encryption.  Source: Economic Times, Delhi  Next step: Organizations should begin inventorying cryptographic assets vulnerable to quantum attacks. Has your enterprise started its quantum migration journey?  5. 635-Crore Scam Network Busted in Gujarat A front-page report in Free Press Journal says six people were arrested by Amreli Police in Gujarat for a cyber fraud network using mobile apps SD Pay and Apna Pay, amassing rupees six hundred thirty‑five crore across multiple bank accounts.  Why it matters: The arrest of six individuals operating mobile app-based fraud platforms SD Pay and Apna Pay highlights the growing sophistication of cyber fraud networks targeting banking customers across India.  Key detail: Amreli Police in Gujarat dismantled the network, which amassed 635 crore rupees across multiple bank accounts through deceptive mobile applications.  Source: Free Press Journal, Mumbai  Next step: Banks and fintech platforms must strengthen customer authentication and fraud detection systems. Are your mobile payment channels adequately protected?  6. Viet Nam Strengthens Data Governance Framework A front-page report in Statesman says Viet Nam is drafting a Law on Data Security, with passage scheduled during the first session of the 16th National Assembly in October. The new law will be the country's fourth data-related law passed over the last two years, complementing the Law on Cybersecurity and the Law on Personal Data Protection which already strengthen measures against cyber threats and data breaches. The law aims to address loopholes in existing regulations by protecting specialised data types in finance, banking, energy, defence and security sectors.  Why it matters: Viet Nam's drafting of a Law on Data Security — its fourth data-related law in two years — signals a regional trend toward comprehensive cyber regulation that Indian enterprises operating in Southeast Asia must monitor.  Key detail: The new law will complement existing cybersecurity and personal data protection laws, addressing loopholes in regulations covering finance, banking, energy, defense, and security sectors. Passage is scheduled during the first session of the 16th National Assembly in October. Under the agreement, an APNIC Resource Public Key Infrastructure repository mirror will be hosted in India and managed by NIXI to reduce latency and improve network resilience. The MoU also focuses on increasing adoption of the IPv6 protocol, with NIXI citing IPv6 penetration in India at almost 80 per cent, the highest in the Asia-Pacific region. Key detail: Under the MoU, an APNIC Resource Public Key Infrastructure repository mirror will be hosted in India, managed by NIXI to reduce latency and improve network resilience. TCS Releases DPDP Act Compliance Report A front-page report in Free Press Journal says TCS released a governance report aligned with the DPDP Act and Rules at the CII Hospital Tech Summit 2026 in Mumbai on Tuesday. We are all using various forms of social media regularly. Although data privacy laws exist, many platforms use this data to train various models. For example, we use facial recognition on our smartphones to unlock the phones. This becomes data for phone manufacturers, which they may use to train (for example) surveillance models. Now, manufacturers like Apple promise that all facial detection data stays local on the iPhone and is never sent to Apple or backed up.  Now, attackers try to identify the data points used to train a particular model. This is called membership inference. They begin by asking whether a particular data point was used in training. Once they can identify an individual, it becomes easy to infer sensitive personal information from the dataset, such as whether the individual has a particular medical syndrome.  So, model builders try to unlearn some of the training data after training the model. This avoids the costly effort of retraining the model (although the gold standard is to fully retrain it after a change in the dataset). However, the process of unlearning particular data points may reveal information about some other data point(s). For example, by analysing the original and changed datasets, the attackers may infer that Alice’s record was removed and Bob’s data was retained (although this is a possible vulnerability rather than an inevitable consequence).
